From Apple's fiscal 2025 Form 10-K (filed October 31, 2025), four developments in the legal/investigative matters described are dated to calendar year 2025. Three appear in Item 3 (Legal Proceedings) and one in the Item 1A risk factors concerning Google, a company with which Apple has commercial relationships.

**1. April 23, 2025 — EU Digital Markets Act (two developments on the same day):**
- The European Commission fined Apple €500 million in the Article 5(4) Investigation (opened March 25, 2024) and issued a cease-and-desist order requiring Apple to remove technical and commercial restrictions preventing developers from steering users to alternative distribution channels outside the App Store. Apple has appealed this decision.
- The Commission also issued preliminary findings in the separate Article 6(4) Investigation (opened June 24, 2024), concerning whether Apple's new contractual requirements for third-party app developers and app marketplaces violate the DMA. A final violation finding could bring a cease-and-desist order and fines up to 10% of Apple's annual worldwide net sales.

**2. April 30, 2025 — Epic Games litigation:**
The U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California found Apple in violation of the 2021 Injunction and enjoined Apple from (a) imposing any commission or fee on purchases consumers make outside an app, (b) restricting, conditioning, limiting, or prohibiting how developers guide consumers to out-of-app purchases, or (c) otherwise interfering with a consumer's choice to proceed in or out of an app. The same day, the court denied Apple's motion to narrow or vacate the 2021 Injunction and referred Apple to the U.S. Attorney for the Northern District of California to determine whether criminal contempt proceedings are appropriate. Apple appealed to the Ninth Circuit.

**3. September 2, 2025 — Google search arrangements (commercial relationship):**
In connection with the August 5, 2024 finding that Google violated U.S. antitrust laws, the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia ordered certain remedies. The order remains subject to further proceedings before that court and to appeal by both the DOJ and Google; a reversal could result in remedies (e.g., prohibiting Google from offering Apple commercial terms for search distribution) that would materially harm Apple's search-licensing revenue.

**4. October 2025 (month only) — Epic Games appeal:**
After its request to stay the April 30 decision pending appeal was denied, Apple's appeal was accepted by the Ninth Circuit on an expedited basis, with oral arguments heard in October 2025.

Not dated to a specific day or month in 2025: Apple notes it settled certain ordinary-course matters during its fiscal fourth quarter of 2025 without material impact, and all other dated developments in these matters (the 2024 openings of the DMA investigations, the March 21, 2024 DOJ lawsuit, the January 16, 2024 compliance filing, the September 30, 2024 motion, and the August 5, 2024 Google liability finding) fall in calendar 2024.

Here are the dividend-related dollar amounts for the 6.00% Series A Mandatory Convertible Preferred Stock given in Boeing's 2024 Form 10-K (excluding the 6.00% rate and $1,000 liquidation preference you noted):

**Up to $345 million per year** (Item 1A, Risk Factors, "Risks Related to Financing and Liquidity")
Boeing states it expects to require up to $345 million of cash per year to pay dividends on the outstanding preferred shares through the mandatory conversion date of October 15, 2027 — i.e., the maximum annual cash outlay for these dividends. (Unpaid dividends accumulate, and if unpaid for six or more dividend periods, preferred holders gain the right to elect two additional directors.)

**$58 million** (Consolidated Statements of Operations, p. 54, and Note 4 – Earnings Per Share)
Labeled "Mandatory convertible preferred stock dividends accumulated during the period," this is the amount of dividends accrued on the preferred stock during 2024 (the shares were issued October 31, 2024, so only a partial period). It is deducted from the $11,817 million net loss attributable to Boeing shareholders to arrive at the $11,875 million net loss attributable to common shareholders and is used in the basic/diluted loss-per-share computation ($18.36).

**$72 million** (Consolidated Statements of Equity, p. 58, and Note 19 – Shareholders' Equity, p. 106)
Dividends of $72 million were declared on the preferred stock in December 2024 to holders of record as of January 1, 2025, and were paid in cash on January 15, 2025. In the Consolidated Statements of Equity it appears as a $72 million reduction of retained earnings ("Cash dividends declared on Mandatory convertible preferred stock").

**$12.50 per share** (Note 19 – Shareholders' Equity)
The per-share amount of that December 2024 declared dividend ($12.50 per share, roughly $72 million across the 5.75 million preferred shares).

Note the distinction between the two period amounts: $58 million is the dividends accumulated (accrued) in 2024 for accounting purposes, while $72 million is the amount declared in December 2024 and paid in cash on January 15, 2025.

JPMorgan Chase's 2023 Form 10-K (which adopted the TDR guidance — ASU 2022-02 — on January 1, 2023 under the modified retrospective method) gives the following amounts, recorded as a cumulative-effect adjustment to opening retained earnings rather than through the income statement:

**Effect on the allowance (Firm total) — $587 million decrease**
- Note 1 (p. 173), Note 13 (p. 256), and the MD&A allowance discussion (p. 131) all state the adoption resulted in a net decrease to the allowance for credit losses of $587 million. This measures the net reduction in the allowance for loan losses as of January 1, 2023 from eliminating TDR accounting: the Firm stopped measuring the allowance for modified loans to troubled borrowers on a discounted-cash-flow, asset-specific basis and applied its non-DCF, portfolio-based allowance approach for all portfolios except collateral-dependent loans and nonaccrual risk-rated loans (for which the DCF/asset-specific approach continues; the adoption did not change the collateral-dependent approach or scope).

**Effect by loan portfolio (in the allowance-for-loan-losses rollforward, "Cumulative effect of a change in accounting principle," MD&A p. 132):**
- Consumer, excluding credit card: $(489) million
- Credit card: $(100) million
- Wholesale: $2 million (an increase)
- Total: $(587) million
These measure how the $587 million reduction was allocated across the Firm's three loan portfolio segments — predominantly residential real estate and credit card, per Notes 1 and 13. No amounts are attributed to individual business segments.

**Effect on retained earnings — $446 million increase (TDR adoption alone)**
- Notes 1 and 13 state the adoption increased retained earnings by $446 million, after-tax. This measures the after-tax cumulative-effect credit to January 1, 2023 retained earnings: the $587 million pretax allowance reduction less the related deferred tax effect (about $141 million).

**Related combined figure — $449 million (both 2023 adoptions)**
- The Consolidated statements of changes in stockholders' equity (p. 169) show a 2023 retained-earnings line "Cumulative effect of change in accounting principles" of $449 million. This measures the combined effect of both standards adopted January 1, 2023 — the TDR guidance ($446 million) plus the Fair Value Hedging – Portfolio Layer Method adoption, whose retained-earnings impact (from the HTM-to-AFS transfer) Note 1 states was not material (roughly $3 million).
